78d85014-3a6d-49f9-b23c-ab04097fe206.one_liner: A close read of the 2s10s curve flattening to ~20bp -- driven now by the long end falling rather than the short end rising -- built around rates, TIPS breakevens, CCC spreads, and IG issuance mix, squarely in the reader's rates/credit wheelhouse.
78d85014-3a6d-49f9-b23c-ab04097fe206.recap: The piece argues the 2-year/10-year Treasury spread has compressed to roughly 20bp, its narrowest in about a year and a half, but stresses the composition matters more than the level: earlier flattening was driven by the 2-year rising (from ~4.2% to ~4.75% since Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech) as the market priced the Fed hiking again on oil-driven inflation fears, including a hike delivered last week and possibly another next month. Recently, though, the 10-year has itself declined, which the host reads as the market beginning to price post-hike demand destruction -- weaker consumption, tighter credit, softer labor -- rather than just Fed reaction function. Supporting evidence cited: Bloomberg options flow betting on SOFR declines, suggesting the 2-year may have overshot the Fed's own dot plot (which points to roughly one more hike, not an open series); PIMCO trimming its long-duration underweight above 5% yields; TIPS breakevens staying contained rather than signaling durable inflation; CCC credit spreads approaching 1100bp; AI infrastructure financing getting harder to distribute; and a striking IG issuance pattern -- Aon's $2bn 30-year drawing ~$10bn of orders, GSK's $500mn 30-year drawing ~10x demand -- yet only ~5% of September IG issuance had 30-year+ maturities, the lowest share since 2020, as issuers favor 5-7 year tenors expecting future refinancing at lower rates while investors scramble for duration. The host invokes the 2008 ECB 'Trichet' analogy of hiking into a weakening economy and lists confirming signals to watch: continued 2s10s and 5s10s compression, contained/declining TIPS breakevens, widening speculative-grade spreads, softening commodities, and deteriorating labor data.

df2bcdc4-b79e-11f1-a9e2-d733ccd909db.one_liner: Former Dallas Fed President Robert Kaplan argues the Fed was right to hike in September but that markets are pricing in more tightening than needed, with the neutral rate near 4-4.25% and credit spreads already well-behaved -- core reading for anyone positioning the front end and curve.
df2bcdc4-b79e-11f1-a9e2-d733ccd909db.recap: Goldman Sachs Exchanges host Alison Nathan interviews Vice Chairman and former Dallas Fed President Robert Kaplan on the Fed's September rate hike under new Chair Kevin Warsh, the first increase in years after three cuts in fall 2025. Kaplan backs the hike, noting month-over-month inflation has run near 3% annualized versus a hoped-for 2.5%, driven partly by an oil shock (crude near $100 versus $60s a year ago) layered on an AI infrastructure boom, strong defense spending, and weak interest-rate-sensitive sectors like autos and housing. He reads the dot plot as muted -- one more 2026 hike, nothing priced for 2027 -- and estimates the nominal neutral rate at roughly 4-4.25%, meaning a further December hike would put policy near neutral with little need for more. He argues markets are pricing in a bigger hiking cycle than warranted, partly as a risk premium against oil staying elevated and uncertainty over Warsh's reaction function. On the real economy, Kaplan flags that the 10-year Treasury is above 5%, driven less by Fed action than by upwardly revised CBO deficit estimates and the absence of a credible fiscal plan; he notes credit spreads and the Treasury curve have already adjusted, arguably pricing in more than the Fed will deliver. He also discusses the Fed's independence (confident it's intact), transparency of officials' reaction functions, the rising share of GDP going to corporate profits versus labor, and how compounding supply shocks (oil, tariffs, immigration-driven labor constraints) complicate the Fed's usual playbook, since rate hikes can't reverse a supply shock but can slow its bleed into broader inflation.

e0c817fa-b712-11f1-be96-0bf9ed46e867.recap: Eric Wallerstein, Chief Macro Strategist at Clock Tower, discusses the Fed's hawkish hike and SEP, noting the 2028 dot rose 50bp and closed a 125bp gap between market and Fed views of neutral. He argues much of the global front-end rate move is actually an oil price effect (oil roughly doubled since January), not a reflection of reaccelerating growth, and that markets are over-extrapolating Q2 strength (which he ties to catch-up bank lending and fiscal stimulus, not a durable trend). He sees fiscal drag, a supply shock, and rate hikes compounding into next year, creating real downside risk the FOMC dismisses. He flags decelerating wage growth and collapsing non-residential construction as signs of mild restrictiveness even amid AI capex. He's watching C&I lending and the Senior Loan Officer Survey as key leading indicators. He increasingly expects a 2022-style bear market (energy shock, valuations, synchronized global tightening, fiscal drag) even while remaining a US growth bull. On other central banks: the BOJ hiked but Ueda sounded dovish, causing yen weakness and a soft intervention; he doubts the BOJ follows through on multiple hikes and prefers being short Japanese belly rates while favoring the Korean won over yen, given South Korea's AI-driven income boom and a hawkish new BOK governor. He dislikes European growth (energy exposure, French fiscal/political risk) despite liking European defense equities, and discusses China's opportunistic oil importing/refining strategy amid the Iran war, which he thinks could run longer than markets expect.

f462d0a2-5837-4195-8aca-cf17994e861b.one_liner: A private-credit direct lending podcast on Hayfin's €15bn European fundraise touches credit-cycle themes (BDC redemption pressure, AI risk in leveraged loan books, 2028/29 maturity wall) relevant to structured credit but has no direct repo/rates angle.
f462d0a2-5837-4195-8aca-cf17994e861b.recap: 9fin's Sunde Jonsson interviews Mark Bickerstaff, co-head of direct lending at Hayfin, following the firm's $15bn fifth direct lending fundraise. Bickerstaff attributes the raise to investor diversification into Europe away from the US, Hayfin's 17-year local origination platform, and an institutional (not retail/BDC) LP base that has insulated it from the scrutiny hitting US semi-liquid vehicles. He estimates US retail/semi-liquid capital is 15-20% of the US private credit market versus under 5% in Europe, though European deal ticket sizes have shrunk this year (from $1bn+ to $200-400m) as US BDCs pull back cross-border allocations — a gap Hayfin's larger fund lets it fill. Borrowers are reportedly now asking lenders about their funding sources and exposure to retail/semi-liquid capital, a new diligence trend favoring locked-up institutional capital. On portfolio health, Hayfin's watch list is at historical-average levels, not elevated, though it is monitoring Middle East-driven oil/inflation pass-through and AI exposure (about 6% of the book in software, 15-20% medium AI risk) via a framework built with consultants since 2024. He flags the 2028/29 maturity wall from high-multiple 2021/22 vintage deals as a coming theme requiring refinancing, structuring, or exit decisions. M&A was subdued in H1 2026 but picked up sharply in July; growth areas cited are tactical/capital solutions (low-teens returns, addressing DPI needs) and asset-based finance (over $12bn deployed historically in real estate, maritime, healthcare).

DPI -- Distributions to Paid-In capital, a private fund performance metric measuring actual cash returned to LPs relative to capital contributed
BSL -- Broadly Syndicated Loan, a leveraged loan distributed to a wide institutional investor base via the syndicated market
